newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS-Dlr/yen risk reversals stay sharply skewed.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS-Dlr/yen risk reversals stay sharply skewed.

text.p: Out-of-the-money yen calls continued to be priced far above equally low-delta yen puts as the dollar nervously vibrated in the lower-112 yen area, just above Monday's six-month low of 111.80 yen, dealers said.
"The market has taken some air out of front-end volatilities, but spot is still at very uncomfortable levels," said Masao Okada, chief options dealer at Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank in New York.
"The downside strikes are so well bid and the upside strikes so battered by spread trades that the 'smile curve' is just a sloping line," he added.

A smile curve reflects implied volatility levels along different strike prices, with the at-the-money delta-50 strike normally the lowest point. The lower the delta for yen puts or calls, the richer the options are priced.
Since Monday, however, one-month 25-delta yen calls have been priced at more than 1.0 point over at-the-money, while 25-delta yen puts stood some 0.8 point below at-the-money.

One-month 25-delta risk reversal, the cost of swapping equally low-delta puts and calls, was quoted at 1.9/2.2 point in favor of yen calls, unchanged from Monday but well above last week's already sharply skewed levels around 1.2/1.6.

Traders said a lag in Japanese exporters' hedging after two years of a dollar-bull market had caused a chain reaction of yen call buying among corporations and resultant dealer short-covering as the dollar slid in the past month.

"It shows how badly positioned the market is. As long as we (spot) stay around these levels, you won't see the skew go away," said a U.S. bank trader in California. "It might actually get worse if we break through 111.80 (yen)."
At-the-money implied volatility for one-month dollar/yen options stood at 13.6/13.8 percent at U.S. midsession, down from Monday's dizzying heights in the upper 14-percent range.
The back end was also a touch easier with one-year off about 0.2 point at 11.1/11.3 percent
Dollar/mark implied volatilities were also softer at the front end, making the curve very flat, as spot drifted slightly higher within familiar ranges mostly between 1.7050 and 1.7200 marks.
Dollar/mark volatilities for one-month out to one-year were lined abreast at around 9.4/9.6 percent after one-month edged down a quarter point.
A hedge fund trader in New York said there was a lot of selling in maturities shorter than a few weeks.
One-month 25-delta risk reversal stood at 0.1/0.3 point in favor of mark puts after flattening to around par on Monday.

Traders said the risk perception was still slightly leaning to the dollar's upside, although sentiment has been swinging back and forth lately due to uncertainty over the fate of European economic and monetary union (EMU).

"In a way, dollar/mark's relatively upward bias has kept dollar/yen from falling sharply in the past few weeks," Okada at DKB said. "It is scary to think what might happen to dollar/yen should dollar/mark start to head lower.
